paper_metadata.title: Knowledge Graphs Generation from Cultural Heritage Texts: Combining LLMs and Ontological Engineering for Scholarly Debates
paper_metadata.abstract: Introduces ATR4CH, a systematic five-step methodology that combines annotation models, ontological frameworks, and LLM-based extraction to generate Cultural Heritage knowledge graphs from text. A sequential pipeline using Claude Sonnet 3.7, Llama 3.3 70B, and GPT-4o-mini is validated on Wikipedia authenticity-assessment debates.

paper_metadata-abstract-05-01.excerpt: This paper introduces ATR4CH (Adaptive Text-to-RDF for Cultural Heritage), a systematic five-step methodology for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Extraction from Cultural Heritage documents.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the gap between rich, interpretative Cultural Heritage scholarly discourse in unstructured texts and sparse structured KGs. It aims to extract agents, competing authenticity claims, evidence, and alternative hypotheses while retaining provenance and multi-perspectival reasoning.

secondary_families: Zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting (without task-specific model training)
methodology.description: ATR4CH is a five-step iterative Text-to-RDF methodology: (I) analyse corpus, target ontology, competency questions, and core ontological patterns; (II) create and validate a minimal working annotation schema and annotation-to-RDF mapping on a pilot corpus; (III) design a modular extraction architecture around that schema; (IV) test end-to-end, refine the production KG annotation model and mappings; (V) extract a held-out test set and perform technical, semantic, competency-based, and expert evaluation. Its case-study implementation is a six-stage sequential pipeline: LLM metadata extraction; GliNER entity detection plus few-shot LLM cognizer classification/coreferences; rule-based Wikidata entity linking; LLM opinion extraction/classification; LLM evidence-feature-evaluation extraction; and LLM hypothesis extraction. JSON-schema outputs are mapped to RDF-star/SEBI graphs.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The target schema is the Scholarly Evidence Based Interpretation ontology (SEBI), combined with RDF-star reification, HiCo InterpretationAct, PROV-O provenance, DCTerms, and linked vocabularies. SEBI models authenticity classifications, alleged metadata, scholarly claims, supporting evidence/features, evaluation criteria/polarity/confidence, and alternative authorship, date, location, and motivation hypotheses. Extraction stages return JSON constrained by schemas and map it to RDF-star; Wikidata and DCMI Type Vocabulary support entity/type alignment.

text_to_kg_stages: Text preprocessing: cleans Wikipedia markup and selects relevant paragraphs
Entity and concept extraction: GliNER detects people, organizations, groups, and locations; LLM identifies CH items and cognizers
Entity typing: entity labels and cognizer/not-cognizer classification
Coreference resolution: LLM extracts additional mentions; mentions are clustered across paragraphs
Entity resolution and linking: rule-based Wikidata candidate retrieval/scoring and owl:sameAs output
Relation and triple extraction: cognizer–item opinions, evidence assessments, and hypothesis relations are extracted
Ontology or schema discovery: corpus/ontology analysis identifies core ontological patterns and competency-question coverage
Graph construction: schema-conformant JSON is mapped to RDF-star/SEBI graphs
Graph validation and correction: mapping validation, end-to-end testing, human review of semantically equivalent false positives, and component/discourse evaluation

input_output.input_type: Raw English Wikipedia articles about Cultural Heritage historical forgeries, hoaxes, and authenticity controversies, stored as markup/text files, with extracted item metadata and selected contextual paragraphs passed between stages.
input_output.input_granularity: Document-level articles are processed first; later stages use entity-centred relevant paragraphs, while the final hypothesis stage uses full document context.
input_output.output_representation: Intermediate JSON objects conforming to component schemas, then RDF-star knowledge graphs implementing SEBI. The graph contains CH items and alleged metadata, Wikidata-linked scholarly agents, HiCo interpretation acts/provenance, quoted authenticity and alternative-hypothesis triples, and evidence nodes with feature assessments and polarity.

models_and_tools: Rule-based entity linking using the Wikibase API, Levenshtein name similarity, type compatibility, and occupation relevance
SEBI ontology; RDF-star; HiCo; PROV-O; DCTerms; Wikidata; DCMI Type Vocabulary
datasets: Case-study corpus: 581 English Wikipedia articles on Cultural Heritage forgeries, hoaxes, and authenticity controversies, collected from 15 Wikipedia categories in October 2024; average 8,150 characters and 1,249 tokens per article
Pilot corpus: Donation of Constantine, Eremin Letter, Getty Kouros, Historia Augusta, Life of Homer, Marriage Charter of Empress Theophanu, and Protocols of the Elders of Sion
Expert-annotated ground truth: 45 CH-item spans, 235 entity spans, 215 interpretation acts, 132 evidences, 115 features, and 308 Wikidata alignments

metrics: Micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 by metadata category; macro-averaged overall metadata scores
Entity-level precision, recall, F1, true positives, false positives, and false negatives
Custom 0–4 evidence score across feature, evaluation perspective, feature class, and polarity; reported mean/percentage
Precision, recall, and F1 for hypothesis/judgment extraction, including type, creator, date, and location F1
G-EVAL debate correctness and debate representativeness on a 0–1 scale
Exploratory SPARQL counts of triples, interpretation acts, and cognizers
baselines: Expert-annotated ground truth (GT), including rehydrated GT for G-EVAL comparison
Comparative model configurations: Claude Sonnet 3.7, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3 70B
evaluation.setting: The authors evaluate three pipeline runs on their manually annotated authenticity-debate data across five evaluation questions: metadata extraction, cognizer recognition, evidence extraction, hypotheses/judgments, and end-to-end discourse fidelity. They manually review metadata false positives for semantic equivalence. Hypothesis evaluation is restricted to successfully matched entities; G-EVAL compares whole rehydrated generated KGs against rehydrated GT. An empirical G-EVAL threshold was derived from three manually reviewed articles.

value: Metadata extraction was strong: Claude overall precision/recall/F1 = 0.987/0.995/0.991; GPT-4o-mini = 0.942/1.000/0.970; Llama 3.3 = 0.933/1.000/0.965.
Cognizer/entity recognition: Claude P/R/F1 = 0.696/0.763/0.728; GPT = 0.718/0.912/0.803; Llama = 0.626/0.817/0.709.
Evidence extraction mean 0–4 scores were Claude 3.87 (96.8%), GPT-4o-mini 3.84 (96.0%), and Llama 3.3 3.81 (95.3%).

Hypothesis macro F1 was Claude 0.655, GPT 0.749, and Llama 0.694. Claude led location hypotheses (0.923) and date hypotheses (0.791); GPT led authenticity-type F1 (0.845); Llama led creator-hypothesis F1 (0.712).
For G-EVAL debate correctness, means were Claude 0.620, GPT 0.590, and Llama 0.533; debate representativeness means were Claude 0.607, GPT 0.580, and Llama 0.523.
Generated KGs contained more triples than GT—Claude 10,173, GPT 12,088, Llama 10,119 versus GT 4,026—while interpretation-act and cognizer counts were broadly comparable.
